titleZh: 酒店月底周转紧，回款和付款要排到同一张表
titleEn: Cash Gets Tight at Month-End: Put Collections and Payments on One Calendar
summaryZh: 账户余额解释不了现金压力。把营收确认、应收、实际回款和刚性付款按同一周期排进四栏时间表，先定位时间错配，再判断经营缺口。
summaryEn: A bank balance cannot explain a cash squeeze. Put revenue recognition, receivables, actual collections and committed payments on one calendar before judging an operating shortfall.
contentZh:
月底经营会开完，报表上的订单和营收都不难看，账户却不敢轻易付款。财务说回款慢，销售说账务压款，收益说渠道结算，采购说供应商已经到期。最后，问题常常被归结为一句“生意不够好”。

先停一下。报表上的营收和手上可用现金不是同一件事。营收确认、回款到账、付款到期，是三条不同的时间线。现金紧张不自动等于订单不够，也不自动等于谁没有催款；它可能来自渠道结算、合同账期、退款争议、付款集中，或真实的经营缺口。

酒店不是靠看账户余额管理现金，而是靠把应收回款和刚性付款放进同一张时间表管理现金。

一、先把三个日期分开

第一是营收确认日：企业按适用会计政策确认收入的日期，不能简单等同于PMS下单、渠道确认或开票日期。第二是实际到账日：钱真正进入账户的日期。第三是付款到期日：工资、供应商、税费和债务等必须支出的日期。

这三条时间线平时分散在不同部门和报表里。单独看，每张表都可能正常；放到同一周期，错配才会出现：本期确认收入，款项尚未到账，而本期的工资和供应商款已经到期。

二、用四栏时间表定位问题

取最近一个完整经营周期，把四类数据逐项勾稽。第一栏为按会计政策确认的营收；第二栏为应收形成日和合同约定回款日；第三栏为银行流水中的实际到账日；第四栏为工资、供应商、税费和债务计划中的刚性付款日。

把四栏排到同一张周历后，将应收标为正常、逾期、争议或暂不可动用。每一笔异常都要能回到来源、责任人和下一日期。这样，现金到底卡在回款、付款节奏还是经营本身，才有证据可判断。

三、三种情况，三种处理顺序

如果应收存在但实际到账普遍晚于合同约定，先检查催收责任、渠道结算规则和争议账；不要直接把它归结为需求问题。

如果营收和回款都正常，但工资、供应商和税费在短时间集中到期，问题首先是付款节奏，需要建立付款优先级和现金预警，而不是把责任推给销售。

如果四栏已经勾稽一致，可动用现金仍然不足，才进入真实经营缺口：重新判断利润、定价、成本和投资回报。账没对齐前就开涨价会或压供应商款，往往只会把时间问题和经营问题混在一起。

四、哪些情况必须单列

新店爬坡、较长的团体合同账期、一次性资本开支、税费、贷款偿还、业主分红和预收款变化，都不能简单塞进日常应收问题。每个酒店的客源结构、合同条件和结算周期不同，不能照搬别家的账龄阈值。融资、税务和合同争议应由有资质的专业人士处理；四栏表是管理工具，不是法律或税务意见。

五、七天做一次最小测试

由总经理牵头，财务制表，销售与收益解释回款条件。七天内完成一个完整经营周期的“营收—应收—回款—付款”四栏表，并连续四周复核。观察逾期应收、平均回款天数、未来刚性付款覆盖情况，以及计划回款与实际到账的偏差。

如果同一笔款在不同记录里的口径对不上，先停止讨论催收目标、涨价或压款，把合同和账务核对一致。先把钱哪天进来、哪天必须出去说清楚，再谈别的。

contentEn:
At the end of the monthly management meeting, orders and reported revenue can look fine while nobody is comfortable approving the next payment. Finance points to slow collections, sales points to the ledger, revenue points to settlement, and procurement points to invoices that are already due. The discussion then collapses into a vague conclusion: business is not good enough.

Stop there. Reported revenue and cash available are not the same thing. Revenue recognition, cash collection and payment due dates are three different timelines. A cash squeeze may come from channel settlement, contractual payment terms, disputed refunds, concentrated payments or a genuine operating shortfall.

A hotel does not manage cash by watching its bank balance. It manages cash by putting receivables and committed payments on one time-based view.

One: keep three dates apart

The revenue-recognition date is the date on which the business recognises revenue under its applicable accounting policy; it should not be assumed to be the same as a PMS booking, channel confirmation or invoice date. The collection date is when cash actually reaches the account. The payment due date is when payroll, suppliers, taxes or debt commitments must be paid.

These timelines often sit in separate departments and separate reports. Each can look normal in isolation. Put them into one operating period and the mismatch becomes visible: revenue is recognised in the current period, cash has not arrived, and current-period wages and suppliers are already due.

Two: reconcile four columns on one calendar

For one complete operating period, reconcile four data sets. Column one is revenue recognised under the accounting policy. Column two is the receivable creation date and the contractual collection date. Column three is the actual collection date in the bank record. Column four is committed payments from payroll, supplier, tax and debt schedules.

Put the columns on one weekly calendar and classify each receivable as normal, overdue, disputed or temporarily unavailable. Each material exception must lead back to a source, an owner and a next date. Only then can a team distinguish a collection issue, a payment-timing issue and an operating shortfall.

Three: three situations require different decisions

When receivables exist but actual collections routinely arrive after the contractual date, begin with collection ownership, settlement rules and disputed items. Do not label it a demand problem before checking the evidence.

When revenue and collections are normal but wages, suppliers and taxes cluster in a short window, the first issue is payment timing. Build a payment priority and cash-warning view instead of placing the burden on sales.

When the four columns reconcile and available cash is still short, the business has reached a genuine operating question: profitability, pricing, cost and return on investment. Calling a pricing meeting or squeezing suppliers before the ledger reconciles only mixes a timing problem with an operating one.

Four: keep certain items out of the daily receivables view

New-hotel ramp-up, longer group-contract payment cycles, one-off capital expenditure, taxes, debt service, owner distributions and changes in advance receipts should be isolated from routine receivables. Client mix, contract terms and settlement cycles vary by property, so another hotel’s ageing threshold cannot be copied. Financing, tax and contract disputes require qualified professional advice; the four-column calendar is a management tool, not legal or tax advice.

Five: run one seven-day minimum test

Have the general manager lead, finance build the table, and sales and revenue explain collection terms. Complete one full-period revenue-receivables-collections-payments calendar within seven days and review it for four consecutive weeks. Watch overdue receivables, average days to collect, coverage of committed payments and variance between planned and actual collections.

If the same item cannot be reconciled across records, stop debating collection targets, pricing or payment pressure and reconcile the contract and ledger first. Say clearly when cash comes in and when it must go out; only then discuss everything else.
